title: Super fixed bond market, equities now the worry
full_text:
When Visy Industries and The Australian Financial Review first joined forces a decade ago to explore what could be done to encourage our superannuation funds to lend more money to local businesses, fixed income was playing second fiddle to equities.
The message from the super funds was that they could not waste their asset allocation budgets on low-returning investments, so the marginal dollars were more likely to be steered towards infrastructure and private equity than direct lending.
Now the conversation has changed dramatically. Fixed income, and private credit in particular, has arguably become too popular as regulators have mounted a rearguard action to make sure all the investor capital that has gushed into the sector has the appropriate protections and disclosures.
Meanwhile, in the capital markets, the Australian corporate bond market that we lamented was underdeveloped is on fire and is growing 200 per cent a year. It is attracting local and international borrowers, while regional institutions are complementing the growing bid from our super funds. If anything, it is the relative health of the equity market we have to be worried about. It is in danger of being crowded out by super funds whose presence on share registers has grown while the number of listed companies is in retreat.
The booming bond market is evidence that the capital markets can flourish on their own without intervention. The problems in the equity market are arguably proof of the converse, particularly if you believe an overly prescriptive performance-testing regime has distorted our local equity markets.
The tension, therefore, is when do our pension system and our capital markets require a helpful nudge in the right direction, and when is it best for us to stay out of the way? For the most part, the superannuation system has naturally evolved to the point where its aggregate interest in fixed income has grown, and in turn enhanced our debt capital markets.
As more Australians approach retirement their risk appetite is moderating, and as they enter retirement their desire for income grows.
The super funds are fully aware they must deliver more annuity-like income for members, and so they need to chase higher yielding but stable fixed income assets.
Don Russell, the chair of AustralianSuper, said risky high-yield debt investing was now part of its fixed income unit, which previously was limited to government and high-grade corporate bonds. This is a recognition of the broader member objective.
It is for this reason that despite the headlines about growing anxiety among retail investors for private credit, the super funds want and need more of it.
There is a catch. Fixed income is not an asset class that is free of risk and the ability of superannuation funds to allocate capital will be tested in a future that will be defined by volatile interest rates, industries facing disruption and a capital expenditure super cycle in which our savings will be aggressively courted.
The other catch, recognised by our super funds, is that fixed income alone is not going to alleviate the anxieties of ageing Australians. We are living longer, and if the last five years are a guide, inflation will pose a persistent threat to our retirement savings.
Capital growth is therefore essential, which means we will still rely on riskier asset classes such as domestic and international equities to do the heavy lifting. We simply cannot escape the reality that for our individual and aggregate prosperity, we will need to take risk.
A well-functioning capital market is one that provides an appropriate reward for risk. The third dimension is liquidity. Here investors expect to be rewarded for their patience when they give up immediate access to their capital. This is why a saver demands the bank pays a higher rate for an extended term deposit.
The banks have been managing liquidity risk for centuries. They borrow money in the short term and lend it in the long term, so are constantly dealing with this so-called mismatch.
As Westpac's Anthony Miller reminded us, our super funds have only ever experienced the weight of money gushing into member accounts and so are relative novices in handling the liquidity challenges.
They are, however, real and have the potential to gnaw at member returns if they are managed poorly. This can either be because super funds are making poor choices and aren't being appropriately rewarded for the patience of their member capital. Or it could be because of poor design.
At times, liquidity is a construct of regulators and policymakers who in times of crisis have been prepared to provide it to the market for the greater good. This is where a nudge has the potential to enhance our capital markets, our pension system and our prosperity, so long as risk is appropriately rewarded.
